derived.us_per_dof_growth: 3,219 -> 10,125 across the large branch, a factor of 3.15
derived.memory_model_MB: 818 fixed + 607 per million DOF. NOTE: this is a two-point line through N=501 and N=1001, not a fit to all three measured points -- N=701 sits 153 MB (9.8%) ABOVE it. Peak memory is linear to about 10%, not better, which is expected of a peak over allocator behaviour. A least-squares line through all three gives 897 + 584 per million DOF and predicts N=1401 about equally well (2.8% vs 2.4%).
derived.memory_verdict: O(DOF) confirmed; the 3.93M DOF case needed 3,280 MB of the A100's 80 GB, so memory is nowhere near the limit
derived.us_per_dof_shape: U-shaped. Falls 19,410 -> 3,219 us/DOF from N=101 to N=501, then rises to 10,125 at N=1401. Minimum at 0.50M DOF.
derived.us_per_dof_note: quote the per-row us_per_dof field, which is the run's own printed figure. Dividing the rounded solve_s by n_dof gives values up to 4 us/DOF different (largest discrepancy at N=501: 3,215 vs 3,219) because solve_s is transcribed rounded. The report's Table 20 uses the us_per_dof field.
derived.cost_breakdown: residual 0.0-0.3%, preconditioner 0.1-0.3%, CG 99.4-99.9%. Read the caveat in the README before quoting this as 'assembly is minimal'.
derived.cost_exponent_note: fitted on the large-DOF branch (N>=501) only; the small-N branch is overhead-dominated and has the opposite slope
derived.memory_prediction_test: the model was built before N=1401 ran and predicted 3,201 MB for its 3.93M DOF; the measured peak was 3,280 MB, an error of 2.4%. The O(DOF) memory claim is therefore not just consistent with the data, it was tested out of sample on a case more than twice as large as anything it had seen, and held. Read this together with memory_model_MB: the line is anchored on two points and N=701 lies 10% off it.
derived.extrapolation_caveat: 818 + 607 per million DOF puts the 40M-DOF reference of section 4.4 at roughly 25 GB. That is a projection ten times beyond the largest case measured here and has NOT been verified.
derived.largest_case: 3,925,602 DOF solved in 11.0 hours using 3,280 MB of the A100's 80 GB

N501_measured_twice.note: identical configuration and identical iteration counts (20 Newton, 40,000 CG, 20 CG failures) on the same A100 model, 13.0% apart in wall clock. Table 20 quotes the root file. This is the run-to-run variation the single-run timings carry and do not otherwise show.

cg_convergence.headline: CG did NOT converge at N>=401: it stopped at the cg_max_iter cap of 2000 on every Newton step. N=101, 201 and 301 converged (cg_failures 0) and those three fix what the true iteration count would have been.
cg_convergence.fit: CG iterations per Newton solve = 5.011 x N, from the three converged rows; the three implied constants (4.992, 5.017, 5.023) span 0.6%. This is the textbook rate: the tangent condition number grows as 1/h^2, so CG needs O(1/h) = O(N) iterations.
cg_convergence.newton_iterations: exactly 20 (2 per load step) for every row where CG did essentially all its work, N=101 through 501. It grows only as truncation deepens: 30 at N=701, 40 at N=1001, 67 at N=1401 -- an inexact Newton direction costs extra Newton steps.
cg_convergence.accuracy_unaffected: Newton's own test is ABSOLUTE (||R|| < 1e-7) and is checked before each step; the counts stay far below the newton_max of 30 per load step. The truncation is a cost defect, not an accuracy defect.
cg_convergence.direction_of_the_error_in_table_20: not one-signed. Truncating CG makes each Newton step cheaper than a converged one, and simultaneously raises the Newton count. Both effects are present at N>=701.
cg_convergence.discovered: 2026-08-29, by reading the stats block the sweep had been writing all along into its own JSON on Drive.
